hints: Start by sorting the polymers into two families: alpha-glucose storage polysaccharides (starch, amylopectin, glycogen) versus beta-glucose structural polysaccharides (cellulose). Which monomer belongs where?
Now think straight chain versus branched chain. 1,4 glycosidic bonds make the straight chain, while 1,6 glycosidic bonds make branch points. Which named polymer is definitely branched?
walkthrough:
**Separate alpha from beta glucose polymers**

Remember this simple rule first. Alpha-glucose builds storage molecules for energy: starch in plants and glycogen in animals. Beta-glucose builds the structural molecule cellulose in plant walls.

So any row that pairs beta-glucose with glycogen, or beta-glucose with cellulose plus branches, is already suspicious.

**Separate straight chains from branched chains**

All these polymers have 1,4 glycosidic bonds joining glucose in a line. Only branched polymers also have 1,6 glycosidic bonds at the branch points.

Amylose is unbranched (1,4 only). Amylopectin and glycogen are both branched (1,4 and 1,6). Cellulose is unbranched (1,4 only).

**Check each row and pick the perfect match**

Row B pairs alpha-glucose with 1,4 and 1,6 bonds to make amylopectin. That is exactly right: amylopectin is the branched part of starch, made from alpha-glucose.

Row A is incomplete because starch as a whole contains both amylose and amylopectin, so not 1,4 only.

options.A: Starch contains both amylose (1,4 only) and amylopectin (1,4 and 1,6), so 1,4 only does not describe whole starch correctly.
options.B: Amylopectin is the branched storage polysaccharide made from alpha-glucose joined by 1,4 bonds in chains and 1,6 bonds at branches.
options.C: Glycogen is made from alpha-glucose, not beta-glucose, even though it is branched with 1,4 and 1,6 bonds.
options.D: Cellulose is made from beta-glucose but it is unbranched with 1,4 bonds only, with no 1,6 branch points.
